title: Iterables and iterators / Generator functions with yield / Generator expressions / Iterator consumption and exhaustion

blocks.text: An iterable supplies an iterator through `iter(value)`. An iterator supplies successive items through `next(iterator)` and signals exhaustion with StopIteration.
Separate `iter(list_value)` calls have separate traversal state; the list stores reusable items.
Calling `iter` on an iterator returns that same iterator, not an independent traversal.
At exhaustion, `next(iterator, default)` returns the default instead of raising StopIteration.

blocks.code:
values = [3, 2]
first = iter(values)
second = iter(values)
print(next(first))
print(next(first))
print(next(first, None))
print(next(second))
print(iter(first) is first)

blocks.text: `(expression for item in iterable if condition)` lazily transforms accepted items. The filtering if clause is optional.
The leftmost iterable expression is evaluated immediately; filtering and item transformations happen during iteration.
As the sole argument to `sum`, a generator expression totals transformed values without an intermediate list.

blocks.text: Each `next(iterator)` consumes an item. A later traversal or consumer sees only what remains.
Once an iterator raises StopIteration, subsequent calls must continue to raise it.
`iter(iterator)` returns the same iterator; it does not reset progress.
For another pass over a reusable collection, obtain a fresh iterator from the collection, not its exhausted iterator.

if True:
    def two_passes(values):
        traversal = iter(values)
        first = list(traversal)
        second = list(iter(traversal))
        return first, second
    # TODO: repair the second pass.

    def trace_exhaustion(values):
        traversal = iter(values)
        first = next(traversal)
        remaining = list(traversal)
        exhausted_once = next(traversal, None)
        exhausted_again = next(traversal, None)
        return first, remaining, exhausted_once, exhausted_again, iter(traversal) is traversal
